oil.summary: Crude collapsed for a second consecutive week as the Iran war-risk premium evaporated. WTI settled at $70.25/bbl (-2.32% on the day, -8.29% on the week, -20.78% on the month) while Brent shed comparable ground to $73.55/bbl, with Middle East benchmarks slipping into contango as Hormuz transit showed signs of recovery. The US suspension of Iran oil sanctions and the announced return of nuclear inspectors drove traders to price in incremental Iranian barrels, more than offsetting Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian facilities in Krasnodar, Ufa, and the Karachaganak processing plant. China's crude imports are tracking their weakest month since 2016 at roughly 6.4 mb/d per Kpler, adding demand-side pressure. Saudi Arabia is expected to cut August official selling prices for Asia. RBOB gasoline bore the sharpest single-day loss at -5.85%, amplifying the bearish signal across the complex.
drivers: US sanctions suspension on Iran and Hormuz flow recovery erasing the conflict risk premium, with Brent down ~10% on the week
China crude imports on pace for weakest month since 2016 (~6.4 mb/d), compressing demand expectations
Saudi Arabia expected to slash August OSPs for Asia; CME options pricing a 77% probability of an OPEC output increase at the next meeting

gas.summary: Natural gas markets sent mixed signals on the day. Henry Hub edged down 1.71% to $3.286/MMBtu but remains up 8.09% on the month, while TTF firmed modestly to €40.65/MWh (+0.61% on the day) though it is still down 12.42% over the past month. The dominant supply-side story was Ukraine's continued long-range drone campaign: strikes on a major Russian natural gas plant were confirmed by multiple sources, and a hit on a Russian processing facility linked to Kazakhstan's Karachaganak field forced a roughly 25% cut in gas output there. Russia's reported attempt to source replacement gasoline from a hesitant Kazakhstan adds to CIS supply stress. Baker Hughes data showed US drillers adding oil and gas rigs this week as Hormuz transit resumes, a mild bearish offset on the US side.
drivers: Ukraine drone strikes on Russian gas processing infrastructure, including Karachaganak-linked facilities, disrupting CIS gas output
Kazakhstan cutting gas production by ~25% following the drone strike on the Russian processing plant it relies on
US rig count rising week-on-week per Baker Hughes, signalling incremental domestic supply growth

power.summary: EU carbon (EUA) was largely unchanged at $75.99/EUA (-0.48% on the day, -0.20% on the week), with a modest +0.46% month-on-month gain offering little directional conviction. TTF's slight daily uptick provides a marginal uplift to gas-fired generation costs but the month-long 12.42% TTF decline keeps fuel-switching pressure subdued. China's new five-year energy plan notably omits restrictions on coal power, framing coal as a 'bottom-line guarantee,' which weighs on any global carbon convergence narrative. Equinor's exit from Japan's offshore wind market signals ongoing retrenchment in renewable expansion by majors. Conversely, a separate report points to AI demand, geopolitical instability, and climate pressure collectively reviving interest in nuclear power globally. The Iran nuclear verification dispute — with conflicting US-Iranian accounts and IAEA access questions unresolved — keeps the geopolitical backdrop unsettled for power sector policy.
drivers: China's new five-year plan preserves coal power growth as a strategic backstop, undermining global decarbonisation momentum
EUA prices flat near $76/EUA with little macro catalyst; month-long TTF decline limiting carbon abatement incentives from fuel switching
Growing nuclear interest driven by AI power demand, war-related energy disruption, and climate pressure, though Iran IAEA access dispute complicates the policy picture
